deep.reconstruction:
This page continues no. 78 from the previous page and then gives nos. 79 and 80. All of it concerns elementary Diophantine problems, mainly from A.m. T. III.

**No. 78, end of the 'autre solution'.** Problem: find x, y, z with x^2+yz, y^2+zx, z^2+xy all squares.
- From the previous page, x=(yz-s^2)/(2s) makes x^2+yz=((yz+s^2)/(2s))^2.
- Setting y^2+xz=(y+pz)^2 gives y=(2p^2 s z+s^2)/(z-4ps) and x=p(p z^2+2s^2)/(z-4ps).
- The third condition becomes a quartic in z. With p=2 the quartic is identically (z^2+8sz+2s^2)^2, so z stays free.
- On this page, p=2 gives y=(8sz+s^2)/(z-8s) and x=(4z^2+4s^2)/(z-8s).
- Euler renames z as t and multiplies everything by t-8s. This gives the two-parameter polynomial family x=4(t^2+s^2), y=s(8t+s), z=t(t-8s). Positivity requires t>8s.
- s=1, t=9 gives (328, 73, 9). The roots are 329, 91, 155 (computed by me).
- s=1, t=13 gives (680, 105, 65) = 5·(136, 21, 13). This is the earlier solution (13, 21, 136) up to permutation, as Euler remarks ('les deux solutions s'accordent').

**No. 79, same problem.**
- The 'special solution' x=a^2-8ab, y=b^2+8ab, z=4a^2+4b^2 is just no. 78's family with t=a, s=b, permuted.
- General ansatz: x=a^2+2b, y=b^2+2a, z=ab(ab-4). Then (my verification) x^2+yz=(a^2+ab^2-2b)^2 and y^2+xz=(b^2+a^2 b-2a)^2 identically.
- So only z^2+xy must be made square. Expanding, this is a^4b^4-(8a^3-2)b^3+17a^2b^2+4ab+2a^3, as printed.
- Euler gives two solutions: (33, 185, 608) and (297, 377, 320).
- My reconstruction: both come from a=2, where the quartic is 16b^4-62b^3+68b^2+8b+16 with square leading and constant terms.
  - b=32/11 is obtained by matching the root 4b^2-(31/4)b+4 (my step). It gives (108/11, 1508/121, 1280/121), which times 121/4 is (297, 377, 320).
  - b=38/3 gives (88/3, 1480/9, 4864/9), which times 9/8 is (33, 185, 608).
- Square roots (mine): 337, 233, 613 for the first triple; 457, 487, 463 for the second.

**No. 80.** Problem: find p, q, r with (p^2+q^2)/2, (p^2+r^2)/2, (q^2+r^2)/2 all squares.
- Five solutions are listed: (89, 191, 329), (97, 553, 833), (119, 833, 1081), (23, 289, 527), (17, 697, 1127).
  - Half-sum roots for (p,q), (p,r), (q,r), all checked by me: 149, 241, 269; 397, 593, 707; 595, 769, 965; 205, 373, 425; 493, 797, 937.
- 'Direct solution': p=(f^2-2g^2)(s^2-2t^2), q=(f^2+2g^2+4fg)(s^2+2t^2+4st)-8fgst.
  - This makes (p^2+q^2)/2 a square identically. My guess for the root, checked numerically at several points: z=(f^2+2fg+2g^2)(s^2+2st+2t^2)+4fgst.
- Changing the signs of g and t leaves p fixed and gives other values, one usable as q and another as r. The one remaining condition is that (q^2+r^2)/2 be square.
  - Example (mine): f=5, g=1, s=3, t=2 gives p=23. The four sign choices give q in {1687, -89, 527, -289}. Taking 289 and 527 reproduces Euler's fourth solution (23, 289, 527).
- Further freedom comes from multiplying by units of Z[√2]. If a^2-2b^2=±1 (Pell pairs (1,1), (3,2), (7,5), (17,12), (41,29), (99,70)), then (af±2bg)^2-2(ag±bf)^2=(a^2-2b^2)(f^2-2g^2) = ±(f^2-2g^2). So f, g can be re-expressed infinitely often, and likewise s, t, with p unchanged up to sign. This continues on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors found. Every printed numerical solution was verified by hand.
No. 78: 'plus grands que les précédents' and the choice t=13 as 'le cas le plus simple' are informal. With s=1, t=13 the triple has common factor 5, which Euler removes.
No. 79: Euler gives no parameter values; the reconstruction a=2, b=38/3 and a=2, b=32/11 is mine.

No. 80: the sign-variation recipe for r does not by itself guarantee (q^2+r^2)/2 is square. Euler says so explicitly ('necesse est'), so this is a search procedure rather than a complete parametrization.
No. 80: 'Hinc solutiones' refers back to material not printed here.

results.what: Two-parameter polynomial solution x=4(t^2+s^2), y=s(8t+s), z=t(t-8s) of x^2+yz, y^2+zx, z^2+xy all squares, obtained because the residual quartic becomes an identical square at p=2
results.modern_name: parametric solution of a system of quadratic Diophantine conditions
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Opera postuma 1862; catalogued in Dickson, History vol. II)

results.what: Ansatz x=a^2+2b, y=b^2+2a, z=ab(ab-4) satisfying two conditions identically, reducing the third to a quartic in b made square by tangent/coefficient matching; yields (33,185,608) and (297,377,320)
results.modern_name: reduction to a quartic y^2=f(b) (genus-1 curve) and finding rational points by the Fermat/Euler method of matching coefficients

results.what: Three squares whose pairwise half-sums are squares; five numerical solutions and a parametric formula for one pair p, q
results.modern_name: squares in arithmetic progression / pairwise-congruum problem (related to Euler-brick type problems)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Op. post.); cf. Dickson, History vol. II

results.what: Composition identity (af+2bg)^2-2(ag+bf)^2=(a^2-2b^2)(f^2-2g^2) and Pell solutions of a^2-2b^2=±1
results.modern_name: Brahmagupta composition identity / units of Z[sqrt2] (Pell equation)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard 18th-century Diophantine manipulations, already published in Euler's Opera postuma (1862) and of the kind catalogued by Dickson. Every number checks out, and the reconstructed parameter choices show nothing beyond routine technique.

checkable.asserts: All three expressions of the no. 78 family are perfect squares of polynomials in s, t.
The no. 79 ansatz satisfies two conditions identically.
The third condition reduces to Euler's printed quartic.
The printed numerical triples satisfy all three square conditions.
The five listed triples of no. 80 have all pairwise half-sums of squares equal to squares.
Euler's direct formula makes (p^2+q^2)/2 a square; the root Z is my conjecture, tested numerically.
The composition identity used at the end of no. 80.
The listed Pell pairs give alternately -1 and +1.
With f=5, s=3 and the sign choices of g, t (p=23), q takes the values 1687, -89, 527, -289, reproducing the solution (23, 289, 527).
